screeningScope: Full-text source, eligibility, study-design, taxonomy, and synthesis-readiness review of frozen 2026-08-01 shortlist queue positions 37-48.

decisionDefinitions.INCLUDE: Eligible for evidence extraction and synthesis after full-text review.
decisionDefinitions.DEGRADED: A required source or verification element was unavailable.

records.sourceFile: Effects of multiple cold-water immersion during pre-season on recovery performance in under-20 male soccer players - A randomized controlled trial.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Twenty-three under-20 male soccer players were randomized during a nine-day preseason to daily post-training cold-water immersion at 10 degrees C for 10 minutes or seated rest. Immersion reduced creatine kinase relative to control, but vertical jump, strength, and perceived recovery did not differ between groups.
records.limitations: The trial was small, short, limited to one under-20 male squad, and used creatine kinase as its primary damage marker. A biochemical difference without corresponding performance or perceived-recovery change does not establish meaningful recovery benefit.
records.synthesisCaution: Do not describe daily cold-water immersion as restoring performance or readiness; the observed benefit was limited to creatine kinase in this short preseason trial.

records.sourceFile: Wake up call for collegiate athlete sleep- narrative review and consensus recommendations from the NCAA Interassociation Task Force on Sleep and Wellness.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: An NCAA interassociation task force combined a narrative review with a Delphi consensus process to recommend annual time-demand review, sleep screening in the preparticipation examination, evidence-based education, and referral pathways for collegiate athletes with sleep concerns.
records.limitations: The paper is a consensus and implementation guide rather than an intervention trial. Several recommendations address institutional practice despite limited collegiate-athlete-specific causal evidence and require local resources and clinical referral capacity.
records.synthesisCaution: Use the recommendations to structure a sleep-support system, not as proof that any single education or screening component will improve performance.

records.sourceFile: Real world fatigue testing in professional rugby union - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: The review included 37 professional male rugby-union studies and meta-analyzed 14. Muscle soreness increased within 96 hours, while pooled changes in jump height, wellness, tiredness, cortisol, and testosterone were generally uncertain or not statistically significant; subjective soreness was the most consistently applicable field measure.
records.limitations: Large within- and between-study variability, inconsistent protocols and time points, mostly observational designs, and male professional samples limited pooled inference. Several objective markers had wide confidence intervals and unclear field utility.
records.synthesisCaution: Favor repeated within-athlete interpretation and a small monitoring battery; do not present a single jump, hormone, heart-rate, or wellness value as a validated fatigue diagnosis.

records.sourceFile: Effect of the length of the microcycle on the daily external load, fatigue, sleep quality, stress, and muscle soreness of professional soccer players - A full-season study.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Daily tracking across a professional soccer season showed that short, regular, and long match-to-match microcycles produced different volume and intensity distributions across training days. Microcycle length did not materially change perceived fatigue, sleep quality, stress, or soreness, and match-day load was largely similar except for high-intensity decelerations.
records.limitations: The observational study represented one professional context, wellness was self-reported, and schedule categories were not randomized. Differences in programmed load cannot be assumed to cause wellness or performance changes.
records.synthesisCaution: Use match spacing to contextualize periodization and monitoring; do not infer readiness from schedule length alone or expect wellness scores to mirror external-load differences.

records.sourceFile: Effects of consecutive domestic and international tournaments on heart rate variability in an elite rugby sevens team.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Ten Olympic-level rugby sevens players recorded waking heart-rate variability and self-reported recovery around consecutive domestic and international tournaments. Self-reported recovery worsened after both tournaments and travel, while heart-rate variability declined more clearly during the international tournament despite similar match-load measures.
records.limitations: The retrospective repeated-measures analysis involved only ten players from one team and could not separate travel, time-zone, schedule, environment, and competition effects. Heart-rate variability responses should not be generalized as universal thresholds.
records.synthesisCaution: Treat travel and tournament context as modifiers of an athlete's own recovery trend; do not attribute the cardiac response to match load alone.

records.sourceFile: A Strategy to Inform Athlete Sleep Support From Questionnaire Data and Its Application in an Elite Athlete Cohort.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: PSQI and Athlete Sleep Behavior Questionnaire data from 412 elite athletes across 27 sports were clustered into three profiles: high-priority poor overall sleep with behavior-focused support, medium-priority disturbance with routine or environment support, and lower-priority acceptable sleep with general support.
records.limitations: The profiles came from one cross-sectional, self-report dataset and qualitative interpretation of k-means clusters. They were not prospectively validated as diagnostic groups or shown to improve sleep when used to assign support.
records.synthesisCaution: Use clustering as a triage aid that prompts individual assessment, not as an automated diagnosis or treatment prescription.

records.sourceFile: Professional athletes have poorer sleep quality and sleep hygiene compared with an age-matched cohort.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Online PSQI and Sleep Hygiene Index responses from 184 professional rugby, netball, and football athletes were compared with 101 age-matched sports-medicine-center attendees. Athletes reported longer sleep duration but more disturbance, poorer regularity and sleep environments, more naps, and difficulty falling asleep after competition.
records.limitations: The cross-sectional self-report design cannot determine whether sport demands caused the differences. The comparator was a sports-medicine-center cohort rather than a population sample, and sport, travel, competition, and demographic effects were not isolated.
records.synthesisCaution: Screen the specific sleep problem and schedule context; do not assume every professional athlete has poor sleep or that group differences establish causation.

records.sourceFile: Sleep quality in elite athletes - Normative values, reliability and understanding contributors to poor sleep.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Among 479 elite athletes across 20 Olympic sports, 52% had PSQI scores of at least five. Sleep-onset latency and perceived sleep quality contributed most to elevated scores, while repeat testing over two months or more showed meaningful within-athlete variability and a minimal detectable change of three points.
records.limitations: The retrospective questionnaire analysis did not objectively measure sleep or diagnose disorders. The sample was female-heavy, sport-specific subgroup sizes varied, and a single PSQI total can conceal different underlying sleep problems.
records.synthesisCaution: Interpret PSQI components and repeat change over time rather than treating one total score or a threshold of five as a definitive diagnosis.

records.sourceFile: Sleep interventions in elite sport - A systematic review.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: A PRISMA-guided review included 32 elite-sport studies of sleep hygiene education, cold exposure, light, supplementation, neurostimulation or neurofeedback, mindfulness, and massage. Sleep education most consistently improved sleep quantity, while some light, supplement, cold-water, and mindfulness studies reported improvements but evidence remained heterogeneous.
records.limitations: Interventions, outcomes, measurement tools, sports, and study quality varied substantially, precluding a single pooled treatment effect. Several intervention categories were supported by few or small studies, and the authors called for more reliable and valid methods.
records.synthesisCaution: Start with individualized sleep assessment and low-risk behavioral or schedule changes; do not rank supplements or technologies as established solutions from this heterogeneous review.

records.sourceFile: The effect of alcohol on subsequent sleep in healthy adults - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Across 27 healthy-adult studies, alcohol delayed REM onset and reduced REM duration, with disruption evident at about two standard drinks and worsening with dose. Only high doses shortened sleep-onset and deep-sleep latency; effects on total sleep time, efficiency, and wake after sleep onset were uncertain.
records.limitations: The evidence was drawn largely from controlled healthy-adult studies rather than athletes in real competition settings. Doses, timing, sex balance, sleep measurement, and study design varied, leaving several whole-night outcomes uncertain.
records.synthesisCaution: Do not frame alcohol as a sleep aid because it may speed sleep onset only at high doses while disrupting REM sleep even at lower doses.

records.sourceFile: Antioxidants for preventing and reducing muscle soreness after exercise- a Cochrane systematic review.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: The Cochrane review included 50 studies and 1,089 participants using antioxidant doses above recommended daily amounts. Any reduction in delayed-onset muscle soreness was smaller than the review's minimal important difference, and 47 trials had high-risk design features; adverse-event reporting was limited.
records.limitations: Most participants were male, supplement types and exercise protocols varied, selective reporting and allocation methods created high risk of bias, and several datasets required estimation. Long-term effects on training adaptation were not established.
records.synthesisCaution: Do not recommend high-dose antioxidants as a meaningful soreness-recovery intervention; consider nutritional adequacy and the potential for concentrated supplementation to alter training adaptation.

records.sourceFile: Compression Garments and Recovery from Exercise- A Meta-Analysis.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: A meta-analysis of 23 studies found a small overall recovery benefit from compression garments, with larger effects for strength recovery after resistance exercise beyond 24 hours and for next-day cycling. Effects by garment pressure and training status remained unclear because reporting was sparse.
records.limitations: The evidence combined small heterogeneous studies, exercise modes, time points, garment types, and outcomes. Pressure and training-status comparisons were underpowered, and pooled effect estimates do not identify an optimal prescription for a specific athlete.
records.synthesisCaution: Compression garments are an optional low-burden adjunct, not a substitute for sleep, fueling, hydration, load management, or condition-specific care.
